explanation: In line 12, free_request(req) is called if body processing fails. However, the function continues to execute. In line 17, update_stats(req->uri, req->method) accesses fields from the freed 'req' pointer. An attacker can trigger a body processing error to cause a Use-After-Free.
When a CLOSE opcode is received, destroy_ws_session(session) frees the session object at line 5. The code then checks session->state at line 8, resulting in a Use-After-Free of the 'session' pointer.

In line 10, 'curr' is freed. In line 12, 'curr = curr->next' attempts to access the 'next' member of the already freed 'curr' structure. This allows an attacker who can force idle connections to crash the daemon or potentially execute code.
In line 7, free_session(s) deallocates the session object. Line 8 then attempts to access s->sid for a debug log message. An attacker manipulating session timing could trigger this UAF.

If terminate_ssl_handshake fails, ssl_cleanup(ssl) is called at line 4, which frees 'ssl'. Line 7 then accesses ssl->error_code. A malicious peer could send a malformed teardown to trigger the failure path.
If cb->one_shot is true, 'cb' is freed at line 5. The code continues to access cb->priority at line 8 and passes the freed 'cb' to other functions in lines 9 or 11.
In line 6, release_node_resources(n) frees the node 'n'. Line 8 then calls get_next_inorder(n), which dereferences the freed node to find its successor in the tree.
If the handshake fails, delete_ws_context(ws) is called at line 4, freeing 'ws'. At line 7, the code checks ws->is_valid, accessing freed memory.
If the full buffer is written, destroy_buffer(src) frees 'src' at line 4. Line 7 then attempts to read src->on_release_cb and line 8 reads src->context from the freed structure.
In line 6, 'c' is freed if it exceeds the idle time. Line 8 then checks c->priority, which is a member of the freed object.

If a session is revoked, it is freed at line 7. The check at line 10 (us->permissions) then accesses this freed memory. This could allow an attacker to bypass authentication checks if they can control the freed memory contents.
In line 6, the header node 'h' is freed. Both the printf at line 8 and the assignment at line 9 (h = h->next) dereference the freed pointer 'h'.
For fatal errors, cleanup_stream(stream) is called at line 5, which frees 'stream'. Line 9 then passes the freed 'stream' pointer to the notification callback handler->notify.
At line 6, 't' is freed if cancelled. Line 9 then accesses t->retry_count and line 10 passes 't' to execute_task, both of which are Use-After-Free conditions.
If ACL check denies the request, teardown_proxy(p) frees 'p' at line 4. Line 7 then checks p->backend_connected, accessing the freed structure.
The body buffer 'b' is freed at line 5 if the reference count is low. At line 9, b->size is accessed to write the access log. An attacker can exploit this via specific response sequences.
If a boundary is found, 'part' is freed at line 5. Line 8 checks part->header_state and line 9 calls resume_parsing(part), both dereferencing the freed memory.
In line 6, the socket structure 's' is freed. Line 9 then checks s->is_readable and line 12 attempts to access s->next. This UAF occurs whenever a socket in the list has an error.
In line 6, the OAuth token 't' is freed. Line 8 then accesses t->is_expired to log the audit message, which is a Use-After-Free of the 't' object.

When the final chunk is parsed, 'c' is freed at line 5. Line 8 then checks c->remaining_bytes and line 9 passes the freed pointer 'c' to append_chunk_data. An attacker can craft a chunked request to exploit this.
